newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-BT, Viag aim for wireless world.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BT, Viag aim for wireless world.

text.p: British Telecom Plc and German utility Viag AG on Thursday shrugged off the abrupt departure of RWE from their telecommunications alliance and said they would step up integration of their German activities.
The cornerstone of their joint business following the defection of power utility RWE AG will be to set up Germany's fourth mobile phone network.
The government tender for the E2 network, in which the BT-Viag alliance appears to be the only bidder, closes next Tuesday with the results to be announced next February.

Should they win the licence as expected because of strong backing from the Bavarian government, they will devote 70 percent of their total investment of six billion marks ($3.92 billion) over the next 10 years to build the E2 network.

BT and Bavarian utility Viag plan to pursue what they see as the new trend in global communications away from owning and operating fixed-wire networks toward a focus on services using a combination of leased lines and wireless networks.

"The industry today is service-driven," said Patrick Gallagher, BT's managing director for Europe. "At the end of the day you do not have to build a lot of infrastructure to be successful in Germany. You need innovative services."

BT and Viag said they were still open to the idea of finding another partner but not a large shareholder like RWE. A Viag official added they would like a partner with marketing and distribution expertise to help their mobile phone business.

Viag chairman Georg Obermeier told reporters the disagreement that led to RWE's departure focused on the viability of a network built around the conversion of mobile and fixed-wire technologies into one seamless network.

Because Viag and BT believe this is the way of the future that would allow them to address a broader group of customers and gain a quick foothold in the residential market, the E2 licence took on a central role in their overall strategy.
"RWE placed much less significance on the strategic importance of this licence," said Obermeier.
Commenting on RWE's decision to leave the group, he added: "We really regretted this. We are not happy that they are gone. This is the end of a cooperation that we entered with a lot of hope."

RWE announced on Wednesday it had decided to defect to a rival venture with energy group Veba and Cable and Wireless. The three companies plan to merge their German telecommunications activities, creating a company worth nearly nine billion marks.

Share traders hammered Viag's stock after the announcement, seeing the company's position on the German telecoms market had weakened. Viag shares fell 6.80 marks to 574.20 in bourse trade on Thursday, while BT were trading by late afternoon in London at 346 pence, down 2.5.
At least one bank, ABN Amro, downgraded Viag to sell from hold because of RWE's departure from the alliance.
But the basic strategy of Viag Interkom, the joint venture between Viag and BT, still remains essentially the same, said Gallagher.
"We want to go for the major business customers down to the smaller businesses and ultimately down to the residential market," he said.
BT and Viag predicted they would win 20 percent of the German mobile phone market, which could have between 12 and 15 million subscribers at the end of the decade.
The E2 network would break even five years after it started-up in 1998 and achieve sales of five billion to six billion marks in 10 years, they said. ($1=1.5315 Mark)
